It is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he gathered his scheme﴾. The rest recited ﴿fa-ajmiʿu﴾ with a cut alif and a kasrah on the mīm. It has two senses. First: the meaning of gathering; the Arabs say ajmaʿtu al-shay' and jamaʿtuhu, meaning the same. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"As if it were at the cliff's edge, a torrent following,
and before it the Dhu al-ʿArjaʾ, gathered by the wind."
[[In the Isfahan copy an addition: i.e., gathered.]]

Second: the meaning of resolve and determination; one says: ajmaʿtu al-amr and azmaʿtuhu, and ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr and azmaʿtu ʿalayhi, when one resolves upon it. A poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit,
whether I will go out one day, and my affair is resolved."

meaning firmly decided. And it is: "resolve your scheme, your plotting, your sorcery and your knowledge."

﴿Then come in a line (saffan)﴾. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: all together. It was also said: in rows. Abu ʿUbayd said: that is, the place of prayer and the assembly. It is related from some eloquent Arabs: "I could not come to the saff yesterday," meaning the place of prayer.

﴿Whoever prevails today will surely succeed﴾: that is, whoever overcomes will win.

They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw﴾. Moses said: ﴿No, you throw first.﴾ ﴿Then their ropes and staffs, by their magic, seemed to him to be moving﴾; ʿasiyy is the plural of ʿasa. Ibn ʿAmir recited "tukhayyilu" with a tā', referring it to the ropes and staffs; the rest recited "yukhayyilu" with a yā', referring it to the scheme or the sorcery. Its meaning: their sorcery made it appear to him, so that he thought ﴿they were moving﴾, that is, walking. They had smeared their ropes and staffs with mercury, and when the heat of the sun struck them they shook and stirred, so Moses thought they were approaching him. ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾: that is, he perceived and found it; it was also said: he concealed it within himself, out of fear. Muqatil said: Moses was only afraid that when the people did the same as he had done, they would cast doubt on his sign, so they would not follow him, and whoever followed him would doubt it.

We said to Moses: ﴿Do not fear, indeed you are the one who prevails﴾, the victor. ﴿And throw what is in your right hand﴾, meaning the staff, ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, to devour and consume it. ﴿What they have made is only a sorcerer's trick﴾. The people of Kufa recited "kaydu sahirin" with a kasrah on the sīn and without an alif; the rest recited "sahirin" with an alif, as the form fa'il. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: attributing the scheme to a man is better than attributing it to sorcery, though that is not prohibited in Arabic.

﴿And the sorcerer does not prosper, wherever he comes﴾ from the earth. It was also said: its meaning is wherever he devises.

﴿So the sorcerers fell down prostrate﴾, saying: ﴿We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.﴾ He (Pharaoh) said: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is used here like His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26]. ﴿Indeed he is your great one, your chief and your teacher who taught you sorcery. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, meaning the left foot and the right hand. ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾, meaning the trunks of the palm trees [[In the Isfahan copy: that is, upon them.]]. Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said:

"They crucified al-ʿAbdi upon the trunk of a palm,
so Shaybān never sneezed except with the ʿAjda'."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 3/277.]]

﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting: ours or the Lord of Moses's.﴾ They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning the hand and the staff, according to Muqatil.

Al-Bayhaqi and al-Isfahani told us, they said: Makki ibn ʿAbdan told us [[In the Isfahan copy: Shuʿayb ibn Muhammad al-Bayhaqi and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani told us: Abu ʿAli ibn ʿAbdan told us.]], saying: Abu al-Azhar narrated to us, saying: Rawh narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Abi ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Barzah, who said: Pharaoh gathered seventy thousand sorcerers, and they cast seventy thousand ropes and seventy thousand staffs, until Moses thought, from their sorcery, that they were moving. God then revealed: ﴿Throw your staff﴾... So he threw his staff and it became a manifest serpent (thuʿban mubin), and it opened its jaws and swallowed their ropes and staffs. At that moment the sorcerers fell down prostrate, and they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their people. At that point they said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning Paradise and Hell, and what they saw of their reward and ranks. [[In the Isfahan copy: the reward and the ranks.]]

He said: Pharaoh's wife used to ask: "Who has won?" It would be said: "Moses has won." She would say: "I believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron." Pharaoh sent for her and said: "Look for the greatest rock you can find, and if she returns from her words, she is his wife; but if she persists in her words, throw the rock upon her." When they came to her, she raised her eyes to heaven and was shown her house in Paradise. She persisted in her words, her soul departed, and her body was thrown down without a soul in it.

﴿And by He who created us﴾, meaning: by Him who created us. It was also said: this is an oath. ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾: judge what you will judge, and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion. ﴿You can only decide upon this worldly life.﴾ That is: "You only rule over us in this world; you have no authority over us except in this world. ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the sorcery you compelled us to practise.﴾ [[In the second copy: you rule over us in this world, so judge what you will judge and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion; you have no authority over us in the Hereafter.]]

Muqatil said: the sorcerers were seventy-two, two of whom were Copts and the chiefs of the group, and seventy of whom were from the Children of Israel. Pharaoh had compelled those seventy from the Children of Israel to learn sorcery.

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Aban said: the sorcerers said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses when he sleeps." So they saw Moses asleep, with his staff guarding him. They said to Pharaoh: "This is not sorcery; a sorcerer's sorcery ceases when he sleeps." But he refused them, except that they should do it. That is His saying: ﴿And what you compelled us to of sorcery﴾. ﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ than you, for you are perishing and doomed.

﴿Indeed whoever comes to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿as a criminal (mujrim)﴾, that is, a polytheist, meaning one who dies in polytheism: ﴿for him is Hell; he will neither die therein, so he may rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him.﴾

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, who dies in faith, ﴿having done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾, the lofty degrees in Paradise: ﴿gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of whoever purifies himself (tazakka)﴾, that is, reforms. It was also said: purifies himself from disbelief and sins. al-Kalbi said: that is, gives the zakah of his soul, and says: "There is no god but God."

From it We created you: that is, your father Adam. ‘Ata' al-Khurasani said: the angel goes and takes some of the dust of the place where the person will be buried, and sprinkles it on the drop (of semen), so he is created from the dust and from the drop. This is His saying, ﴿From it We created you﴾.

﴿And into it We will return you﴾: that is, at death and burial.

Ali said: "When the angel takes the soul of a believer, he ascends with it to heaven and says: 'O Lord, Your servant so-and-so, we have taken his soul.' He says: 'Return them, for I have promised him: ﴿From it We created you and into it We will return you﴾.' He hears the sound of their sandals as they turn their backs and leave." [[al-Musannaf li-Ibn Abi Shaybah: 3/254.]]

﴿And from it We will bring you forth once more﴾: another time, after death, at the Resurrection.

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾: that is, Pharaoh; all of them, namely the hand, the staff and the nine signs. ﴿But he denied them and refused.﴾ He claimed they were sorcery and refused to submit. ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery, O Moses? So we will surely bring you sorcery like it. Set between us and you an appointment﴾, that is, fix between us and you a term and a time ﴿which neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, will not exceed, ﴿in a place equitable (suwa)﴾, meaning level/open. Al-Hasan, ʿAsim, al-Aʿmash and Hamzah recited sawan with a ḍammah on the sīn; the rest with a kasrah. Both are dialects, like ʿidan and ʿidan, and ṭuwa and ṭuwa.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: a just place between us and you. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a clear open place. al-Kalbi said: other than this place. Abu ʿUbayd and al-Qaysi said: a middle point between the two groups. Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi said:

"Indeed our father had settled in a town
equidistant between Qays and Qays of ʿAylan, and al-Fazar."

Al-Fazar: Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

He (Moses) said: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that is, the Day of ʿAshura'.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was a festival day for them every year, when they would adorn themselves and gather.

Jaʿfar related from Saʿid, who said: it was a market day for them. It was also said: it was the day of Nawruz.

Al-Hasan and Hubayrah on the authority of Hafs recited ﴿yawm al-zinah﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning "on the day"; the rest recited it with ḍammah as a subject and predicate.

﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾: at the time of mid-morning, when they gather openly in daylight, so that the proof is more conclusive and further from doubt. ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his scheme﴾, his tricks, and his sorcerers. ﴿Then he came to the appointment.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they were seventy-two sorcerers, each with a rope and a staff. It was also said they were four hundred.

Moses said to the sorcerers: ﴿Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾. The people of Kufa recited ﴿fayuḥṭikakum﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā' [[In the Isfahan copy: the tā'.]] and a kasrah on the ḥā'; the rest with a fatḥah on both. Both are dialects: saḥta and asḥta.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿will destroy you﴾; Qatadah said: will root you out; Abu Salih said: will slaughter you. al-Farazdaq said:

"The age has bitten, O son of Marwan, and left
of wealth only what is wiped out or what is worn away."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 2/224.]] [[In the Isfahan copy: "only what is a trace or swears."]]

﴿Then they disputed their affair among themselves and conferred in secret﴾: al-najwa means private conversation, and it may be a noun or a verbal noun. ﴿They said: "Indeed these two are only sorcerers."﴾ ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud) recited: "wa-asarru al-najwa, inna hadhani la-sahiran" with the alif of inna pronounced with a fatḥah and the nūn of ḥadhani... Ibn Kathir and Hafs recited ﴿inna hadhani la-sahirani﴾ with a kasrah on the alif of inna and a jazm on the nūn, with the alif in hadhani, meaning "these two are nothing but sorcerers," like the saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 186]. [[In the Isfahan copy an addition: meaning: we do not think you are other than among the liars.]] A poet said:

"May your mother lose you, for you have killed none but a Muslim;
the punishment of the Merciful has descended upon you."

Meaning: you have killed none but a Muslim. The validity of this reading is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "inna dhan la-sahiran" [[In the Isfahan copy: "inna dhan la-sahiran."]]. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafi and Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ [[In the Isfahan copy: Abu ʿAmr al-ʿAlaʾ.]] recited "inna hadhayni la-sahiran" with a yā', according to the original form. Abu ʿAmr said: "I am ashamed before God to recite 'inna hadhani'." The rest recited inna with tashdid and hadhani with an alif, and they differed about it.

Some people said, based on what Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbdus and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid told us, that they said: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Asamm narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm al-Samari narrated to us, saying: al-Farra' narrated to us, saying: Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿAʾishah, that she was asked about God's saying in al-Nisa': ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 162], and about His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], and about His saying: ﴿Indeed these two are sorcerers﴾ [Taha: 63]. She said: "O nephew, this is an error of the scribe."

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: "There is a solecism in the Mushaf, and the Arabs will correct it with their tongues."

Aban said: this verse was recited in front of ʿUthman, and he said: "A solecism and an error." It was said to him: "Why did you not change it?" He said:
"Leave it, for it does not make lawful what is forbidden, nor forbid what is lawful."

Others said: this is the dialect of al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, Zabid and Kinanah, who make the two dual forms (alif) in the nominative, accusative and genitive with alif.

al-Farra' said: a man from the Banu al-Asad recited to me, and I have never seen anyone more eloquent than him:

"He lowered his head like the lowering of a snake; if it sees
a place for its fangs, the serpent would deafen it."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 7/92; the wording is: "fa-atraqa ... wa-law yara ... li-nabayhi."]]

And they say: "kusirat yadahu" (his two hands were broken), and "rakibat ʿalahu" (he rode upon his back), meaning yadayhi and ʿalayhi. A poet said:

"He provided himself from us a blow between his ears,
which called him to the dust of a barren desert."

He meant between his two ears. Another said:

"What she-camel of a rider do we see?
They flew over her and a bird flew over her."

meaning over them and over her. Another said:

"Indeed her father and her father's father
have reached the furthest point in glory."

It is related that a Bedouin asked Ibn al-Zubayr for something, and he refused it. He said: "May God curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said: "Indeed, and its owner," meaning yes. A poet said:

"My blamers rose early to reproach me, and I reproach them,
and they say: 'Grey hair has covered you and you have grown old,' so I said: 'Indeed.'"

meaning yes. al-Farra' said: there is another interpretation: that one says the alif is a support for this, staying in its place and never disappearing in any situation, as the Arabs say: "alladhi" then they added a nūn to indicate the plural, and so they said: "alladhun" in its nominative, accusative and genitive, and in the oblique case they say "alladhun."

﴿They want to drive you out of your land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with their sorcery, and to take away your excellent way (al-muthla)﴾. Al-Shaʿbi related from ʿAli, who said: they would turn people's faces toward themselves; it is in Syriac.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, the chiefs and nobles of your people. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: the best and most excellent of those with judgement and intellect.

ʿIkrimah said: that is, your best people will go away.

Qatadah said: your excellent way that day; the Children of Israel at that time were the greatest in number and wealth. The enemy of God said: "They only want to take it for themselves."

al-Kisa'i said: ﴿bi-tariqatikum﴾ means by your custom, your guidance and your manner; and al-muthla is an adjective of al-tariqah, as in your saying: "imra'ah kubra" (a great woman). The Arabs say: "fulan ʿala al-tariqah al-muthla," meaning on the upright guidance. A poet said:

"How many scattered people were afflicted with ignorance,
whom desire drove to deviation, and they were led astray,
and deviated from the best way and went astray,
and the crowd of loss and the lines of ruin cast them down,
so feet slipped in it and they came to a fire
whose brains boiled from it."

al-Muthla is the feminine of al-amthal.

﴿So gather your scheme﴾: Abu ʿAmr recited "fa-ajmiʿu" with a connecting alif and a fatḥah on the mīm, from jamaʿa, meaning: leave nothing of your scheme unless you bring it. It is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he gathered his scheme﴾. The rest recited ﴿fa-ajmiʿu﴾ with a cut alif and a kasrah on the mīm. It has two senses. First: the meaning of gathering; the Arabs say ajmaʿtu al-shay' and jamaʿtuhu, meaning the same. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"As if it were at the cliff's edge, a torrent following,
and before it the Dhu al-ʿArjaʾ, gathered by the wind."
[[In the Isfahan copy an addition: i.e., gathered.]]

Second: the meaning of resolve and determination; one says: ajmaʿtu al-amr and azmaʿtuhu, and ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr and azmaʿtu ʿalayhi, when one resolves upon it. A poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit,
whether I will go out one day, and my affair is resolved."

meaning firmly decided. And it is: "resolve your scheme, your plotting, your sorcery and your knowledge."

﴿Then come in a line (saffan)﴾. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: all together. It was also said: in rows. Abu ʿUbayd said: that is, the place of prayer and the assembly. It is related from some eloquent Arabs: "I could not come to the saff yesterday," meaning the place of prayer.

﴿Whoever prevails today will surely succeed﴾: that is, whoever overcomes will win.

They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw﴾. Moses said: ﴿No, you throw first.﴾ ﴿Then their ropes and staffs, by their magic, seemed to him to be moving﴾; ʿasiyy is the plural of ʿasa. Ibn ʿAmir recited "tukhayyilu" with a tā', referring it to the ropes and staffs; the rest recited "yukhayyilu" with a yā', referring it to the scheme or the sorcery. Its meaning: their sorcery made it appear to him, so that he thought ﴿they were moving﴾, that is, walking. They had smeared their ropes and staffs with mercury, and when the heat of the sun struck them they shook and stirred, so Moses thought they were approaching him. ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾: that is, he perceived and found it; it was also said: he concealed it within himself, out of fear. Muqatil said: Moses was only afraid that when the people did the same as he had done, they would cast doubt on his sign, so they would not follow him, and whoever followed him would doubt it.

We said to Moses: ﴿Do not fear, indeed you are the one who prevails﴾, the victor. ﴿And throw what is in your right hand﴾, meaning the staff, ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, to devour and consume it. ﴿What they have made is only a sorcerer's trick﴾. The people of Kufa recited "kaydu sahirin" with a kasrah on the sīn and without an alif; the rest recited "sahirin" with an alif, as the form fa'il. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: attributing the scheme to a man is better than attributing it to sorcery, though that is not prohibited in Arabic.

﴿And the sorcerer does not prosper, wherever he comes﴾ from the earth. It was also said: its meaning is wherever he devises.

﴿So the sorcerers fell down prostrate﴾, saying: ﴿We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.﴾ He (Pharaoh) said: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is used here like His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26]. ﴿Indeed he is your great one, your chief and your teacher who taught you sorcery. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, meaning the left foot and the right hand. ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾, meaning the trunks of the palm trees [[In the Isfahan copy: that is, upon them.]]. Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said:

"They crucified al-ʿAbdi upon the trunk of a palm,
so Shaybān never sneezed except with the ʿAjda'."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 3/277.]]

﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting: ours or the Lord of Moses's.﴾ They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning the hand and the staff, according to Muqatil.

Al-Bayhaqi and al-Isfahani told us, they said: Makki ibn ʿAbdan told us [[In the Isfahan copy: Shuʿayb ibn Muhammad al-Bayhaqi and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani told us: Abu ʿAli ibn ʿAbdan told us.]], saying: Abu al-Azhar narrated to us, saying: Rawh narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Abi ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Barzah, who said: Pharaoh gathered seventy thousand sorcerers, and they cast seventy thousand ropes and seventy thousand staffs, until Moses thought, from their sorcery, that they were moving. God then revealed: ﴿Throw your staff﴾... So he threw his staff and it became a manifest serpent (thuʿban mubin), and it opened its jaws and swallowed their ropes and staffs. At that moment the sorcerers fell down prostrate, and they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their people. At that point they said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning Paradise and Hell, and what they saw of their reward and ranks. [[In the Isfahan copy: the reward and the ranks.]]

He said: Pharaoh's wife used to ask: "Who has won?" It would be said: "Moses has won." She would say: "I believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron." Pharaoh sent for her and said: "Look for the greatest rock you can find, and if she returns from her words, she is his wife; but if she persists in her words, throw the rock upon her." When they came to her, she raised her eyes to heaven and was shown her house in Paradise. She persisted in her words, her soul departed, and her body was thrown down without a soul in it.

﴿And by He who created us﴾, meaning: by Him who created us. It was also said: this is an oath. ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾: judge what you will judge, and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion. ﴿You can only decide upon this worldly life.﴾ That is: "You only rule over us in this world; you have no authority over us except in this world. ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the sorcery you compelled us to practise.﴾ [[In the second copy: you rule over us in this world, so judge what you will judge and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion; you have no authority over us in the Hereafter.]]

Muqatil said: the sorcerers were seventy-two, two of whom were Copts and the chiefs of the group, and seventy of whom were from the Children of Israel. Pharaoh had compelled those seventy from the Children of Israel to learn sorcery.

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Aban said: the sorcerers said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses when he sleeps." So they saw Moses asleep, with his staff guarding him. They said to Pharaoh: "This is not sorcery; a sorcerer's sorcery ceases when he sleeps." But he refused them, except that they should do it. That is His saying: ﴿And what you compelled us to of sorcery﴾. ﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ than you, for you are perishing and doomed.

﴿Indeed whoever comes to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿as a criminal (mujrim)﴾, that is, a polytheist, meaning one who dies in polytheism: ﴿for him is Hell; he will neither die therein, so he may rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him.﴾

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, who dies in faith, ﴿having done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾, the lofty degrees in Paradise: ﴿gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of whoever purifies himself (tazakka)﴾, that is, reforms. It was also said: purifies himself from disbelief and sins. al-Kalbi said: that is, gives the zakah of his soul, and says: "There is no god but God."

From it We created you: that is, your father Adam. ‘Ata' al-Khurasani said: the angel goes and takes some of the dust of the place where the person will be buried, and sprinkles it on the drop (of semen), so he is created from the dust and from the drop. This is His saying, ﴿From it We created you﴾.

﴿And into it We will return you﴾: that is, at death and burial.

Ali said: "When the angel takes the soul of a believer, he ascends with it to heaven and says: 'O Lord, Your servant so-and-so, we have taken his soul.' He says: 'Return them, for I have promised him: ﴿From it We created you and into it We will return you﴾.' He hears the sound of their sandals as they turn their backs and leave." [[al-Musannaf li-Ibn Abi Shaybah: 3/254.]]

﴿And from it We will bring you forth once more﴾: another time, after death, at the Resurrection.

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾: that is, Pharaoh; all of them, namely the hand, the staff and the nine signs. ﴿But he denied them and refused.﴾ He claimed they were sorcery and refused to submit. ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery, O Moses? So we will surely bring you sorcery like it. Set between us and you an appointment﴾, that is, fix between us and you a term and a time ﴿which neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, will not exceed, ﴿in a place equitable (suwa)﴾, meaning level/open. Al-Hasan, ʿAsim, al-Aʿmash and Hamzah recited sawan with a ḍammah on the sīn; the rest with a kasrah. Both are dialects, like ʿidan and ʿidan, and ṭuwa and ṭuwa.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: a just place between us and you. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a clear open place. al-Kalbi said: other than this place. Abu ʿUbayd and al-Qaysi said: a middle point between the two groups. Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi said:

"Indeed our father had settled in a town
equidistant between Qays and Qays of ʿAylan, and al-Fazar."

Al-Fazar: Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

He (Moses) said: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that is, the Day of ʿAshura'.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was a festival day for them every year, when they would adorn themselves and gather.

Jaʿfar related from Saʿid, who said: it was a market day for them. It was also said: it was the day of Nawruz.

Al-Hasan and Hubayrah on the authority of Hafs recited ﴿yawm al-zinah﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning "on the day"; the rest recited it with ḍammah as a subject and predicate.

﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾: at the time of mid-morning, when they gather openly in daylight, so that the proof is more conclusive and further from doubt. ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his scheme﴾, his tricks, and his sorcerers. ﴿Then he came to the appointment.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they were seventy-two sorcerers, each with a rope and a staff. It was also said they were four hundred.

Moses said to the sorcerers: ﴿Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾. The people of Kufa recited ﴿fayuḥṭikakum﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā' [[In the Isfahan copy: the tā'.]] and a kasrah on the ḥā'; the rest with a fatḥah on both. Both are dialects: saḥta and asḥta.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿will destroy you﴾; Qatadah said: will root you out; Abu Salih said: will slaughter you. al-Farazdaq said:

"The age has bitten, O son of Marwan, and left
of wealth only what is wiped out or what is worn away."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 2/224.]] [[In the Isfahan copy: "only what is a trace or swears."]]

﴿Then they disputed their affair among themselves and conferred in secret﴾: al-najwa means private conversation, and it may be a noun or a verbal noun. ﴿They said: "Indeed these two are only sorcerers."﴾ ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud) recited: "wa-asarru al-najwa, inna hadhani la-sahiran" with the alif of inna pronounced with a fatḥah and the nūn of ḥadhani... Ibn Kathir and Hafs recited ﴿inna hadhani la-sahirani﴾ with a kasrah on the alif of inna and a jazm on the nūn, with the alif in hadhani, meaning "these two are nothing but sorcerers," like the saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 186]. [[In the Isfahan copy an addition: meaning: we do not think you are other than among the liars.]] A poet said:

"May your mother lose you, for you have killed none but a Muslim;
the punishment of the Merciful has descended upon you."

Meaning: you have killed none but a Muslim. The validity of this reading is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "inna dhan la-sahiran" [[In the Isfahan copy: "inna dhan la-sahiran."]]. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafi and Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ [[In the Isfahan copy: Abu ʿAmr al-ʿAlaʾ.]] recited "inna hadhayni la-sahiran" with a yā', according to the original form. Abu ʿAmr said: "I am ashamed before God to recite 'inna hadhani'." The rest recited inna with tashdid and hadhani with an alif, and they differed about it.

Some people said, based on what Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbdus and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid told us, that they said: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Asamm narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm al-Samari narrated to us, saying: al-Farra' narrated to us, saying: Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿAʾishah, that she was asked about God's saying in al-Nisa': ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 162], and about His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], and about His saying: ﴿Indeed these two are sorcerers﴾ [Taha: 63]. She said: "O nephew, this is an error of the scribe."

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: "There is a solecism in the Mushaf, and the Arabs will correct it with their tongues."

Aban said: this verse was recited in front of ʿUthman, and he said: "A solecism and an error." It was said to him: "Why did you not change it?" He said:
"Leave it, for it does not make lawful what is forbidden, nor forbid what is lawful."

Others said: this is the dialect of al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, Zabid and Kinanah, who make the two dual forms (alif) in the nominative, accusative and genitive with alif.

al-Farra' said: a man from the Banu al-Asad recited to me, and I have never seen anyone more eloquent than him:

"He lowered his head like the lowering of a snake; if it sees
a place for its fangs, the serpent would deafen it."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 7/92; the wording is: "fa-atraqa ... wa-law yara ... li-nabayhi."]]

And they say: "kusirat yadahu" (his two hands were broken), and "rakibat ʿalahu" (he rode upon his back), meaning yadayhi and ʿalayhi. A poet said:

"He provided himself from us a blow between his ears,
which called him to the dust of a barren desert."

He meant between his two ears. Another said:

"What she-camel of a rider do we see?
They flew over her and a bird flew over her."

meaning over them and over her. Another said:

"Indeed her father and her father's father
have reached the furthest point in glory."

It is related that a Bedouin asked Ibn al-Zubayr for something, and he refused it. He said: "May God curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said: "Indeed, and its owner," meaning yes. A poet said:

"My blamers rose early to reproach me, and I reproach them,
and they say: 'Grey hair has covered you and you have grown old,' so I said: 'Indeed.'"

meaning yes. al-Farra' said: there is another interpretation: that one says the alif is a support for this, staying in its place and never disappearing in any situation, as the Arabs say: "alladhi" then they added a nūn to indicate the plural, and so they said: "alladhun" in its nominative, accusative and genitive, and in the oblique case they say "alladhun."

﴿They want to drive you out of your land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with their sorcery, and to take away your excellent way (al-muthla)﴾. Al-Shaʿbi related from ʿAli, who said: they would turn people's faces toward themselves; it is in Syriac.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, the chiefs and nobles of your people. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: the best and most excellent of those with judgement and intellect.

ʿIkrimah said: that is, your best people will go away.

Qatadah said: your excellent way that day; the Children of Israel at that time were the greatest in number and wealth. The enemy of God said: "They only want to take it for themselves."

al-Kisa'i said: ﴿bi-tariqatikum﴾ means by your custom, your guidance and your manner; and al-muthla is an adjective of al-tariqah, as in your saying: "imra'ah kubra" (a great woman). The Arabs say: "fulan ʿala al-tariqah al-muthla," meaning on the upright guidance. A poet said:

"How many scattered people were afflicted with ignorance,
whom desire drove to deviation, and they were led astray,
and deviated from the best way and went astray,
and the crowd of loss and the lines of ruin cast them down,
so feet slipped in it and they came to a fire
whose brains boiled from it."

al-Muthla is the feminine of al-amthal.

﴿So gather your scheme﴾: Abu ʿAmr recited "fa-ajmiʿu" with a connecting alif and a fatḥah on the mīm, from jamaʿa, meaning: leave nothing of your scheme unless you bring it. It is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he gathered his scheme﴾. The rest recited ﴿fa-ajmiʿu﴾ with a cut alif and a kasrah on the mīm. It has two senses. First: the meaning of gathering; the Arabs say ajmaʿtu al-shay' and jamaʿtuhu, meaning the same. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"As if it were at the cliff's edge, a torrent following,
and before it the Dhu al-ʿArjaʾ, gathered by the wind."
[[In the Isfahan copy an addition: i.e., gathered.]]

Second: the meaning of resolve and determination; one says: ajmaʿtu al-amr and azmaʿtuhu, and ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr and azmaʿtu ʿalayhi, when one resolves upon it. A poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit,
whether I will go out one day, and my affair is resolved."

meaning firmly decided. And it is: "resolve your scheme, your plotting, your sorcery and your knowledge."

﴿Then come in a line (saffan)﴾. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: all together. It was also said: in rows. Abu ʿUbayd said: that is, the place of prayer and the assembly. It is related from some eloquent Arabs: "I could not come to the saff yesterday," meaning the place of prayer.

﴿Whoever prevails today will surely succeed﴾: that is, whoever overcomes will win.

They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw﴾. Moses said: ﴿No, you throw first.﴾ ﴿Then their ropes and staffs, by their magic, seemed to him to be moving﴾; ʿasiyy is the plural of ʿasa. Ibn ʿAmir recited "tukhayyilu" with a tā', referring it to the ropes and staffs; the rest recited "yukhayyilu" with a yā', referring it to the scheme or the sorcery. Its meaning: their sorcery made it appear to him, so that he thought ﴿they were moving﴾, that is, walking. They had smeared their ropes and staffs with mercury, and when the heat of the sun struck them they shook and stirred, so Moses thought they were approaching him. ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾: that is, he perceived and found it; it was also said: he concealed it within himself, out of fear. Muqatil said: Moses was only afraid that when the people did the same as he had done, they would cast doubt on his sign, so they would not follow him, and whoever followed him would doubt it.

We said to Moses: ﴿Do not fear, indeed you are the one who prevails﴾, the victor. ﴿And throw what is in your right hand﴾, meaning the staff, ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, to devour and consume it. ﴿What they have made is only a sorcerer's trick﴾. The people of Kufa recited "kaydu sahirin" with a kasrah on the sīn and without an alif; the rest recited "sahirin" with an alif, as the form fa'il. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: attributing the scheme to a man is better than attributing it to sorcery, though that is not prohibited in Arabic.

﴿And the sorcerer does not prosper, wherever he comes﴾ from the earth. It was also said: its meaning is wherever he devises.

﴿So the sorcerers fell down prostrate﴾, saying: ﴿We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.﴾ He (Pharaoh) said: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is used here like His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26]. ﴿Indeed he is your great one, your chief and your teacher who taught you sorcery. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, meaning the left foot and the right hand. ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾, meaning the trunks of the palm trees [[In the Isfahan copy: that is, upon them.]]. Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said:

"They crucified al-ʿAbdi upon the trunk of a palm,
so Shaybān never sneezed except with the ʿAjda'."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 3/277.]]

﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting: ours or the Lord of Moses's.﴾ They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning the hand and the staff, according to Muqatil.

Al-Bayhaqi and al-Isfahani told us, they said: Makki ibn ʿAbdan told us [[In the Isfahan copy: Shuʿayb ibn Muhammad al-Bayhaqi and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani told us: Abu ʿAli ibn ʿAbdan told us.]], saying: Abu al-Azhar narrated to us, saying: Rawh narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Abi ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Barzah, who said: Pharaoh gathered seventy thousand sorcerers, and they cast seventy thousand ropes and seventy thousand staffs, until Moses thought, from their sorcery, that they were moving. God then revealed: ﴿Throw your staff﴾... So he threw his staff and it became a manifest serpent (thuʿban mubin), and it opened its jaws and swallowed their ropes and staffs. At that moment the sorcerers fell down prostrate, and they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their people. At that point they said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning Paradise and Hell, and what they saw of their reward and ranks. [[In the Isfahan copy: the reward and the ranks.]]

He said: Pharaoh's wife used to ask: "Who has won?" It would be said: "Moses has won." She would say: "I believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron." Pharaoh sent for her and said: "Look for the greatest rock you can find, and if she returns from her words, she is his wife; but if she persists in her words, throw the rock upon her." When they came to her, she raised her eyes to heaven and was shown her house in Paradise. She persisted in her words, her soul departed, and her body was thrown down without a soul in it.

﴿And by He who created us﴾, meaning: by Him who created us. It was also said: this is an oath. ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾: judge what you will judge, and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion. ﴿You can only decide upon this worldly life.﴾ That is: "You only rule over us in this world; you have no authority over us except in this world. ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the sorcery you compelled us to practise.﴾ [[In the second copy: you rule over us in this world, so judge what you will judge and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion; you have no authority over us in the Hereafter.]]

Muqatil said: the sorcerers were seventy-two, two of whom were Copts and the chiefs of the group, and seventy of whom were from the Children of Israel. Pharaoh had compelled those seventy from the Children of Israel to learn sorcery.

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Aban said: the sorcerers said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses when he sleeps." So they saw Moses asleep, with his staff guarding him. They said to Pharaoh: "This is not sorcery; a sorcerer's sorcery ceases when he sleeps." But he refused them, except that they should do it. That is His saying: ﴿And what you compelled us to of sorcery﴾. ﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ than you, for you are perishing and doomed.

﴿Indeed whoever comes to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿as a criminal (mujrim)﴾, that is, a polytheist, meaning one who dies in polytheism: ﴿for him is Hell; he will neither die therein, so he may rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him.﴾

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, who dies in faith, ﴿having done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾, the lofty degrees in Paradise: ﴿gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of whoever purifies himself (tazakka)﴾, that is, reforms. It was also said: purifies himself from disbelief and sins. al-Kalbi said: that is, gives the zakah of his soul, and says: "There is no god but God."

From it We created you: that is, your father Adam. ‘Ata' al-Khurasani said: the angel goes and takes some of the dust of the place where the person will be buried, and sprinkles it on the drop (of semen), so he is created from the dust and from the drop. This is His saying, ﴿From it We created you﴾.

﴿And into it We will return you﴾: that is, at death and burial.

Ali said: "When the angel takes the soul of a believer, he ascends with it to heaven and says: 'O Lord, Your servant so-and-so, we have taken his soul.' He says: 'Return them, for I have promised him: ﴿From it We created you and into it We will return you﴾.' He hears the sound of their sandals as they turn their backs and leave." [[al-Musannaf li-Ibn Abi Shaybah: 3/254.]]

﴿And from it We will bring you forth once more﴾: another time, after death, at the Resurrection.

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾: that is, Pharaoh; all of them, namely the hand, the staff and the nine signs. ﴿But he denied them and refused.﴾ He claimed they were sorcery and refused to submit. ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery, O Moses? So we will surely bring you sorcery like it. Set between us and you an appointment﴾, that is, fix between us and you a term and a time ﴿which neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, will not exceed, ﴿in a place equitable (suwa)﴾, meaning level/open. Al-Hasan, ʿAsim, al-Aʿmash and Hamzah recited sawan with a ḍammah on the sīn; the rest with a kasrah. Both are dialects, like ʿidan and ʿidan, and ṭuwa and ṭuwa.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: a just place between us and you. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a clear open place. al-Kalbi said: other than this place. Abu ʿUbayd and al-Qaysi said: a middle point between the two groups. Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi said:

"Indeed our father had settled in a town
equidistant between Qays and Qays of ʿAylan, and al-Fazar."

Al-Fazar: Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

He (Moses) said: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that is, the Day of ʿAshura'.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was a festival day for them every year, when they would adorn themselves and gather.

Jaʿfar related from Saʿid, who said: it was a market day for them. It was also said: it was the day of Nawruz.

Al-Hasan and Hubayrah on the authority of Hafs recited ﴿yawm al-zinah﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning "on the day"; the rest recited it with ḍammah as a subject and predicate.

﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾: at the time of mid-morning, when they gather openly in daylight, so that the proof is more conclusive and further from doubt. ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his scheme﴾, his tricks, and his sorcerers. ﴿Then he came to the appointment.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they were seventy-two sorcerers, each with a rope and a staff. It was also said they were four hundred.

Moses said to the sorcerers: ﴿Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾. The people of Kufa recited ﴿fayuḥṭikakum﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā' [[In the Isfahan copy: the tā'.]] and a kasrah on the ḥā'; the rest with a fatḥah on both. Both are dialects: saḥta and asḥta.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿will destroy you﴾; Qatadah said: will root you out; Abu Salih said: will slaughter you. al-Farazdaq said:

"The age has bitten, O son of Marwan, and left
of wealth only what is wiped out or what is worn away."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 2/224.]] [[In the Isfahan copy: "only what is a trace or swears."]]

﴿Then they disputed their affair among themselves and conferred in secret﴾: al-najwa means private conversation, and it may be a noun or a verbal noun. ﴿They said: "Indeed these two are only sorcerers."﴾ ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud) recited: "wa-asarru al-najwa, inna hadhani la-sahiran" with the alif of inna pronounced with a fatḥah and the nūn of ḥadhani... Ibn Kathir and Hafs recited ﴿inna hadhani la-sahirani﴾ with a kasrah on the alif of inna and a jazm on the nūn, with the alif in hadhani, meaning "these two are nothing but sorcerers," like the saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 186]. [[In the Isfahan copy an addition: meaning: we do not think you are other than among the liars.]] A poet said:

"May your mother lose you, for you have killed none but a Muslim;
the punishment of the Merciful has descended upon you."

Meaning: you have killed none but a Muslim. The validity of this reading is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "inna dhan la-sahiran" [[In the Isfahan copy: "inna dhan la-sahiran."]]. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafi and Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ [[In the Isfahan copy: Abu ʿAmr al-ʿAlaʾ.]] recited "inna hadhayni la-sahiran" with a yā', according to the original form. Abu ʿAmr said: "I am ashamed before God to recite 'inna hadhani'." The rest recited inna with tashdid and hadhani with an alif, and they differed about it.

Some people said, based on what Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbdus and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid told us, that they said: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Asamm narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm al-Samari narrated to us, saying: al-Farra' narrated to us, saying: Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿAʾishah, that she was asked about God's saying in al-Nisa': ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 162], and about His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], and about His saying: ﴿Indeed these two are sorcerers﴾ [Taha: 63]. She said: "O nephew, this is an error of the scribe."

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: "There is a solecism in the Mushaf, and the Arabs will correct it with their tongues."

Aban said: this verse was recited in front of ʿUthman, and he said: "A solecism and an error." It was said to him: "Why did you not change it?" He said:
"Leave it, for it does not make lawful what is forbidden, nor forbid what is lawful."

Others said: this is the dialect of al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, Zabid and Kinanah, who make the two dual forms (alif) in the nominative, accusative and genitive with alif.

al-Farra' said: a man from the Banu al-Asad recited to me, and I have never seen anyone more eloquent than him:

"He lowered his head like the lowering of a snake; if it sees
a place for its fangs, the serpent would deafen it."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 7/92; the wording is: "fa-atraqa ... wa-law yara ... li-nabayhi."]]

And they say: "kusirat yadahu" (his two hands were broken), and "rakibat ʿalahu" (he rode upon his back), meaning yadayhi and ʿalayhi. A poet said:

"He provided himself from us a blow between his ears,
which called him to the dust of a barren desert."

He meant between his two ears. Another said:

"What she-camel of a rider do we see?
They flew over her and a bird flew over her."

meaning over them and over her. Another said:

"Indeed her father and her father's father
have reached the furthest point in glory."

It is related that a Bedouin asked Ibn al-Zubayr for something, and he refused it. He said: "May God curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said: "Indeed, and its owner," meaning yes. A poet said:

"My blamers rose early to reproach me, and I reproach them,
and they say: 'Grey hair has covered you and you have grown old,' so I said: 'Indeed.'"

meaning yes. al-Farra' said: there is another interpretation: that one says the alif is a support for this, staying in its place and never disappearing in any situation, as the Arabs say: "alladhi" then they added a nūn to indicate the plural, and so they said: "alladhun" in its nominative, accusative and genitive, and in the oblique case they say "alladhun."

﴿They want to drive you out of your land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with their sorcery, and to take away your excellent way (al-muthla)﴾. Al-Shaʿbi related from ʿAli, who said: they would turn people's faces toward themselves; it is in Syriac.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, the chiefs and nobles of your people. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: the best and most excellent of those with judgement and intellect.

ʿIkrimah said: that is, your best people will go away.

Qatadah said: your excellent way that day; the Children of Israel at that time were the greatest in number and wealth. The enemy of God said: "They only want to take it for themselves."

al-Kisa'i said: ﴿bi-tariqatikum﴾ means by your custom, your guidance and your manner; and al-muthla is an adjective of al-tariqah, as in your saying: "imra'ah kubra" (a great woman). The Arabs say: "fulan ʿala al-tariqah al-muthla," meaning on the upright guidance. A poet said:

"How many scattered people were afflicted with ignorance,
whom desire drove to deviation, and they were led astray,
and deviated from the best way and went astray,
and the crowd of loss and the lines of ruin cast them down,
so feet slipped in it and they came to a fire
whose brains boiled from it."

al-Muthla is the feminine of al-amthal.

﴿So gather your scheme﴾: Abu ʿAmr recited "fa-ajmiʿu" with a connecting alif and a fatḥah on the mīm, from jamaʿa, meaning: leave nothing of your scheme unless you bring it. It is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he gathered his scheme﴾. The rest recited ﴿fa-ajmiʿu﴾ with a cut alif and a kasrah on the mīm. It has two senses. First: the meaning of gathering; the Arabs say ajmaʿtu al-shay' and jamaʿtuhu, meaning the same. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"As if it were at the cliff's edge, a torrent following,
and before it the Dhu al-ʿArjaʾ, gathered by the wind."
[[In the Isfahan copy an addition: i.e., gathered.]]

Second: the meaning of resolve and determination; one says: ajmaʿtu al-amr and azmaʿtuhu, and ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr and azmaʿtu ʿalayhi, when one resolves upon it. A poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit,
whether I will go out one day, and my affair is resolved."

meaning firmly decided. And it is: "resolve your scheme, your plotting, your sorcery and your knowledge."

﴿Then come in a line (saffan)﴾. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: all together. It was also said: in rows. Abu ʿUbayd said: that is, the place of prayer and the assembly. It is related from some eloquent Arabs: "I could not come to the saff yesterday," meaning the place of prayer.

﴿Whoever prevails today will surely succeed﴾: that is, whoever overcomes will win.

They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw﴾. Moses said: ﴿No, you throw first.﴾ ﴿Then their ropes and staffs, by their magic, seemed to him to be moving﴾; ʿasiyy is the plural of ʿasa. Ibn ʿAmir recited "tukhayyilu" with a tā', referring it to the ropes and staffs; the rest recited "yukhayyilu" with a yā', referring it to the scheme or the sorcery. Its meaning: their sorcery made it appear to him, so that he thought ﴿they were moving﴾, that is, walking. They had smeared their ropes and staffs with mercury, and when the heat of the sun struck them they shook and stirred, so Moses thought they were approaching him. ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾: that is, he perceived and found it; it was also said: he concealed it within himself, out of fear. Muqatil said: Moses was only afraid that when the people did the same as he had done, they would cast doubt on his sign, so they would not follow him, and whoever followed him would doubt it.

We said to Moses: ﴿Do not fear, indeed you are the one who prevails﴾, the victor. ﴿And throw what is in your right hand﴾, meaning the staff, ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, to devour and consume it. ﴿What they have made is only a sorcerer's trick﴾. The people of Kufa recited "kaydu sahirin" with a kasrah on the sīn and without an alif; the rest recited "sahirin" with an alif, as the form fa'il. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: attributing the scheme to a man is better than attributing it to sorcery, though that is not prohibited in Arabic.

﴿And the sorcerer does not prosper, wherever he comes﴾ from the earth. It was also said: its meaning is wherever he devises.

﴿So the sorcerers fell down prostrate﴾, saying: ﴿We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.﴾ He (Pharaoh) said: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is used here like His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26]. ﴿Indeed he is your great one, your chief and your teacher who taught you sorcery. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, meaning the left foot and the right hand. ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾, meaning the trunks of the palm trees [[In the Isfahan copy: that is, upon them.]]. Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said:

"They crucified al-ʿAbdi upon the trunk of a palm,
so Shaybān never sneezed except with the ʿAjda'."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 3/277.]]

﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting: ours or the Lord of Moses's.﴾ They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning the hand and the staff, according to Muqatil.

Al-Bayhaqi and al-Isfahani told us, they said: Makki ibn ʿAbdan told us [[In the Isfahan copy: Shuʿayb ibn Muhammad al-Bayhaqi and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani told us: Abu ʿAli ibn ʿAbdan told us.]], saying: Abu al-Azhar narrated to us, saying: Rawh narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Abi ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Barzah, who said: Pharaoh gathered seventy thousand sorcerers, and they cast seventy thousand ropes and seventy thousand staffs, until Moses thought, from their sorcery, that they were moving. God then revealed: ﴿Throw your staff﴾... So he threw his staff and it became a manifest serpent (thuʿban mubin), and it opened its jaws and swallowed their ropes and staffs. At that moment the sorcerers fell down prostrate, and they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their people. At that point they said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning Paradise and Hell, and what they saw of their reward and ranks. [[In the Isfahan copy: the reward and the ranks.]]

He said: Pharaoh's wife used to ask: "Who has won?" It would be said: "Moses has won." She would say: "I believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron." Pharaoh sent for her and said: "Look for the greatest rock you can find, and if she returns from her words, she is his wife; but if she persists in her words, throw the rock upon her." When they came to her, she raised her eyes to heaven and was shown her house in Paradise. She persisted in her words, her soul departed, and her body was thrown down without a soul in it.

﴿And by He who created us﴾, meaning: by Him who created us. It was also said: this is an oath. ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾: judge what you will judge, and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion. ﴿You can only decide upon this worldly life.﴾ That is: "You only rule over us in this world; you have no authority over us except in this world. ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the sorcery you compelled us to practise.﴾ [[In the second copy: you rule over us in this world, so judge what you will judge and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion; you have no authority over us in the Hereafter.]]

Muqatil said: the sorcerers were seventy-two, two of whom were Copts and the chiefs of the group, and seventy of whom were from the Children of Israel. Pharaoh had compelled those seventy from the Children of Israel to learn sorcery.

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Aban said: the sorcerers said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses when he sleeps." So they saw Moses asleep, with his staff guarding him. They said to Pharaoh: "This is not sorcery; a sorcerer's sorcery ceases when he sleeps." But he refused them, except that they should do it. That is His saying: ﴿And what you compelled us to of sorcery﴾. ﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ than you, for you are perishing and doomed.

﴿Indeed whoever comes to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿as a criminal (mujrim)﴾, that is, a polytheist, meaning one who dies in polytheism: ﴿for him is Hell; he will neither die therein, so he may rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him.﴾

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, who dies in faith, ﴿having done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾, the lofty degrees in Paradise: ﴿gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of whoever purifies himself (tazakka)﴾, that is, reforms. It was also said: purifies himself from disbelief and sins. al-Kalbi said: that is, gives the zakah of his soul, and says: "There is no god but God."

From it We created you: that is, your father Adam. ‘Ata' al-Khurasani said: the angel goes and takes some of the dust of the place where the person will be buried, and sprinkles it on the drop (of semen), so he is created from the dust and from the drop. This is His saying, ﴿From it We created you﴾.

﴿And into it We will return you﴾: that is, at death and burial.

Ali said: "When the angel takes the soul of a believer, he ascends with it to heaven and says: 'O Lord, Your servant so-and-so, we have taken his soul.' He says: 'Return them, for I have promised him: ﴿From it We created you and into it We will return you﴾.' He hears the sound of their sandals as they turn their backs and leave." [[al-Musannaf li-Ibn Abi Shaybah: 3/254.]]

﴿And from it We will bring you forth once more﴾: another time, after death, at the Resurrection.

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾: that is, Pharaoh; all of them, namely the hand, the staff and the nine signs. ﴿But he denied them and refused.﴾ He claimed they were sorcery and refused to submit. ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery, O Moses? So we will surely bring you sorcery like it. Set between us and you an appointment﴾, that is, fix between us and you a term and a time ﴿which neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, will not exceed, ﴿in a place equitable (suwa)﴾, meaning level/open. Al-Hasan, ʿAsim, al-Aʿmash and Hamzah recited sawan with a ḍammah on the sīn; the rest with a kasrah. Both are dialects, like ʿidan and ʿidan, and ṭuwa and ṭuwa.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: a just place between us and you. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a clear open place. al-Kalbi said: other than this place. Abu ʿUbayd and al-Qaysi said: a middle point between the two groups. Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi said:

"Indeed our father had settled in a town
equidistant between Qays and Qays of ʿAylan, and al-Fazar."

Al-Fazar: Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

He (Moses) said: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that is, the Day of ʿAshura'.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was a festival day for them every year, when they would adorn themselves and gather.

Jaʿfar related from Saʿid, who said: it was a market day for them. It was also said: it was the day of Nawruz.

Al-Hasan and Hubayrah on the authority of Hafs recited ﴿yawm al-zinah﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning "on the day"; the rest recited it with ḍammah as a subject and predicate.

﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾: at the time of mid-morning, when they gather openly in daylight, so that the proof is more conclusive and further from doubt. ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his scheme﴾, his tricks, and his sorcerers. ﴿Then he came to the appointment.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they were seventy-two sorcerers, each with a rope and a staff. It was also said they were four hundred.

Moses said to the sorcerers: ﴿Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾. The people of Kufa recited ﴿fayuḥṭikakum﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā' [[In the Isfahan copy: the tā'.]] and a kasrah on the ḥā'; the rest with a fatḥah on both. Both are dialects: saḥta and asḥta.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿will destroy you﴾; Qatadah said: will root you out; Abu Salih said: will slaughter you. al-Farazdaq said:

"The age has bitten, O son of Marwan, and left
of wealth only what is wiped out or what is worn away."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 2/224.]] [[In the Isfahan copy: "only what is a trace or swears."]]

﴿Then they disputed their affair among themselves and conferred in secret﴾: al-najwa means private conversation, and it may be a noun or a verbal noun. ﴿They said: "Indeed these two are only sorcerers."﴾ ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud) recited: "wa-asarru al-najwa, inna hadhani la-sahiran" with the alif of inna pronounced with a fatḥah and the nūn of ḥadhani... Ibn Kathir and Hafs recited ﴿inna hadhani la-sahirani﴾ with a kasrah on the alif of inna and a jazm on the nūn, with the alif in hadhani, meaning "these two are nothing but sorcerers," like the saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 186]. [[In the Isfahan copy an addition: meaning: we do not think you are other than among the liars.]] A poet said:

"May your mother lose you, for you have killed none but a Muslim;
the punishment of the Merciful has descended upon you."

Meaning: you have killed none but a Muslim. The validity of this reading is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "inna dhan la-sahiran" [[In the Isfahan copy: "inna dhan la-sahiran."]]. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafi and Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ [[In the Isfahan copy: Abu ʿAmr al-ʿAlaʾ.]] recited "inna hadhayni la-sahiran" with a yā', according to the original form. Abu ʿAmr said: "I am ashamed before God to recite 'inna hadhani'." The rest recited inna with tashdid and hadhani with an alif, and they differed about it.

Some people said, based on what Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbdus and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid told us, that they said: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Asamm narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm al-Samari narrated to us, saying: al-Farra' narrated to us, saying: Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿAʾishah, that she was asked about God's saying in al-Nisa': ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 162], and about His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], and about His saying: ﴿Indeed these two are sorcerers﴾ [Taha: 63]. She said: "O nephew, this is an error of the scribe."

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: "There is a solecism in the Mushaf, and the Arabs will correct it with their tongues."

Aban said: this verse was recited in front of ʿUthman, and he said: "A solecism and an error." It was said to him: "Why did you not change it?" He said:
"Leave it, for it does not make lawful what is forbidden, nor forbid what is lawful."

Others said: this is the dialect of al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, Zabid and Kinanah, who make the two dual forms (alif) in the nominative, accusative and genitive with alif.

al-Farra' said: a man from the Banu al-Asad recited to me, and I have never seen anyone more eloquent than him:

"He lowered his head like the lowering of a snake; if it sees
a place for its fangs, the serpent would deafen it."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 7/92; the wording is: "fa-atraqa ... wa-law yara ... li-nabayhi."]]

And they say: "kusirat yadahu" (his two hands were broken), and "rakibat ʿalahu" (he rode upon his back), meaning yadayhi and ʿalayhi. A poet said:

"He provided himself from us a blow between his ears,
which called him to the dust of a barren desert."

He meant between his two ears. Another said:

"What she-camel of a rider do we see?
They flew over her and a bird flew over her."

meaning over them and over her. Another said:

"Indeed her father and her father's father
have reached the furthest point in glory."

It is related that a Bedouin asked Ibn al-Zubayr for something, and he refused it. He said: "May God curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said: "Indeed, and its owner," meaning yes. A poet said:

"My blamers rose early to reproach me, and I reproach them,
and they say: 'Grey hair has covered you and you have grown old,' so I said: 'Indeed.'"

meaning yes. al-Farra' said: there is another interpretation: that one says the alif is a support for this, staying in its place and never disappearing in any situation, as the Arabs say: "alladhi" then they added a nūn to indicate the plural, and so they said: "alladhun" in its nominative, accusative and genitive, and in the oblique case they say "alladhun."

﴿They want to drive you out of your land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with their sorcery, and to take away your excellent way (al-muthla)﴾. Al-Shaʿbi related from ʿAli, who said: they would turn people's faces toward themselves; it is in Syriac.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, the chiefs and nobles of your people. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: the best and most excellent of those with judgement and intellect.

ʿIkrimah said: that is, your best people will go away.

Qatadah said: your excellent way that day; the Children of Israel at that time were the greatest in number and wealth. The enemy of God said: "They only want to take it for themselves."

al-Kisa'i said: ﴿bi-tariqatikum﴾ means by your custom, your guidance and your manner; and al-muthla is an adjective of al-tariqah, as in your saying: "imra'ah kubra" (a great woman). The Arabs say: "fulan ʿala al-tariqah al-muthla," meaning on the upright guidance. A poet said:

"How many scattered people were afflicted with ignorance,
whom desire drove to deviation, and they were led astray,
and deviated from the best way and went astray,
and the crowd of loss and the lines of ruin cast them down,
so feet slipped in it and they came to a fire
whose brains boiled from it."

al-Muthla is the feminine of al-amthal.

﴿So gather your scheme﴾: Abu ʿAmr recited "fa-ajmiʿu" with a connecting alif and a fatḥah on the mīm, from jamaʿa, meaning: leave nothing of your scheme unless you bring it. It is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he gathered his scheme﴾. The rest recited ﴿fa-ajmiʿu﴾ with a cut alif and a kasrah on the mīm. It has two senses. First: the meaning of gathering; the Arabs say ajmaʿtu al-shay' and jamaʿtuhu, meaning the same. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"As if it were at the cliff's edge, a torrent following,
and before it the Dhu al-ʿArjaʾ, gathered by the wind."
[[In the Isfahan copy an addition: i.e., gathered.]]

Second: the meaning of resolve and determination; one says: ajmaʿtu al-amr and azmaʿtuhu, and ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr and azmaʿtu ʿalayhi, when one resolves upon it. A poet said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit,
whether I will go out one day, and my affair is resolved."

meaning firmly decided. And it is: "resolve your scheme, your plotting, your sorcery and your knowledge."

﴿Then come in a line (saffan)﴾. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: all together. It was also said: in rows. Abu ʿUbayd said: that is, the place of prayer and the assembly. It is related from some eloquent Arabs: "I could not come to the saff yesterday," meaning the place of prayer.

﴿Whoever prevails today will surely succeed﴾: that is, whoever overcomes will win.

They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw﴾. Moses said: ﴿No, you throw first.﴾ ﴿Then their ropes and staffs, by their magic, seemed to him to be moving﴾; ʿasiyy is the plural of ʿasa. Ibn ʿAmir recited "tukhayyilu" with a tā', referring it to the ropes and staffs; the rest recited "yukhayyilu" with a yā', referring it to the scheme or the sorcery. Its meaning: their sorcery made it appear to him, so that he thought ﴿they were moving﴾, that is, walking. They had smeared their ropes and staffs with mercury, and when the heat of the sun struck them they shook and stirred, so Moses thought they were approaching him. ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾: that is, he perceived and found it; it was also said: he concealed it within himself, out of fear. Muqatil said: Moses was only afraid that when the people did the same as he had done, they would cast doubt on his sign, so they would not follow him, and whoever followed him would doubt it.

We said to Moses: ﴿Do not fear, indeed you are the one who prevails﴾, the victor. ﴿And throw what is in your right hand﴾, meaning the staff, ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, to devour and consume it. ﴿What they have made is only a sorcerer's trick﴾. The people of Kufa recited "kaydu sahirin" with a kasrah on the sīn and without an alif; the rest recited "sahirin" with an alif, as the form fa'il. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: attributing the scheme to a man is better than attributing it to sorcery, though that is not prohibited in Arabic.

﴿And the sorcerer does not prosper, wherever he comes﴾ from the earth. It was also said: its meaning is wherever he devises.

﴿So the sorcerers fell down prostrate﴾, saying: ﴿We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.﴾ He (Pharaoh) said: ﴿Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?﴾ It is used here like His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26]. ﴿Indeed he is your great one, your chief and your teacher who taught you sorcery. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, meaning the left foot and the right hand. ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾, meaning the trunks of the palm trees [[In the Isfahan copy: that is, upon them.]]. Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said:

"They crucified al-ʿAbdi upon the trunk of a palm,
so Shaybān never sneezed except with the ʿAjda'."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 3/277.]]

﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting: ours or the Lord of Moses's.﴾ They (the sorcerers) said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning the hand and the staff, according to Muqatil.

Al-Bayhaqi and al-Isfahani told us, they said: Makki ibn ʿAbdan told us [[In the Isfahan copy: Shuʿayb ibn Muhammad al-Bayhaqi and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani told us: Abu ʿAli ibn ʿAbdan told us.]], saying: Abu al-Azhar narrated to us, saying: Rawh narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Abi ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Barzah, who said: Pharaoh gathered seventy thousand sorcerers, and they cast seventy thousand ropes and seventy thousand staffs, until Moses thought, from their sorcery, that they were moving. God then revealed: ﴿Throw your staff﴾... So he threw his staff and it became a manifest serpent (thuʿban mubin), and it opened its jaws and swallowed their ropes and staffs. At that moment the sorcerers fell down prostrate, and they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their people. At that point they said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾, meaning Paradise and Hell, and what they saw of their reward and ranks. [[In the Isfahan copy: the reward and the ranks.]]

He said: Pharaoh's wife used to ask: "Who has won?" It would be said: "Moses has won." She would say: "I believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron." Pharaoh sent for her and said: "Look for the greatest rock you can find, and if she returns from her words, she is his wife; but if she persists in her words, throw the rock upon her." When they came to her, she raised her eyes to heaven and was shown her house in Paradise. She persisted in her words, her soul departed, and her body was thrown down without a soul in it.

﴿And by He who created us﴾, meaning: by Him who created us. It was also said: this is an oath. ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾: judge what you will judge, and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion. ﴿You can only decide upon this worldly life.﴾ That is: "You only rule over us in this world; you have no authority over us except in this world. ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the sorcery you compelled us to practise.﴾ [[In the second copy: you rule over us in this world, so judge what you will judge and do what you will do of cutting and crucifixion; you have no authority over us in the Hereafter.]]

Muqatil said: the sorcerers were seventy-two, two of whom were Copts and the chiefs of the group, and seventy of whom were from the Children of Israel. Pharaoh had compelled those seventy from the Children of Israel to learn sorcery.

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Aban said: the sorcerers said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses when he sleeps." So they saw Moses asleep, with his staff guarding him. They said to Pharaoh: "This is not sorcery; a sorcerer's sorcery ceases when he sleeps." But he refused them, except that they should do it. That is His saying: ﴿And what you compelled us to of sorcery﴾. ﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ than you, for you are perishing and doomed.

﴿Indeed whoever comes to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿as a criminal (mujrim)﴾, that is, a polytheist, meaning one who dies in polytheism: ﴿for him is Hell; he will neither die therein, so he may rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him.﴾

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾, who dies in faith, ﴿having done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾, the lofty degrees in Paradise: ﴿gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of whoever purifies himself (tazakka)﴾, that is, reforms. It was also said: purifies himself from disbelief and sins. al-Kalbi said: that is, gives the zakah of his soul, and says: "There is no god but God."

From it We created you: that is, your father Adam. ‘Ata' al-Khurasani said: the angel goes and takes some of the dust of the place where the person will be buried, and sprinkles it on the drop (of semen), so he is created from the dust and from the drop. This is His saying, ﴿From it We created you﴾.

﴿And into it We will return you﴾: that is, at death and burial.

Ali said: "When the angel takes the soul of a believer, he ascends with it to heaven and says: 'O Lord, Your servant so-and-so, we have taken his soul.' He says: 'Return them, for I have promised him: ﴿From it We created you and into it We will return you﴾.' He hears the sound of their sandals as they turn their backs and leave." [[al-Musannaf li-Ibn Abi Shaybah: 3/254.]]

﴿And from it We will bring you forth once more﴾: another time, after death, at the Resurrection.

﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾: that is, Pharaoh; all of them, namely the hand, the staff and the nine signs. ﴿But he denied them and refused.﴾ He claimed they were sorcery and refused to submit. ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, that is, Egypt, ﴿with your sorcery, O Moses? So we will surely bring you sorcery like it. Set between us and you an appointment﴾, that is, fix between us and you a term and a time ﴿which neither we nor you will fail to keep﴾, that is, will not exceed, ﴿in a place equitable (suwa)﴾, meaning level/open. Al-Hasan, ʿAsim, al-Aʿmash and Hamzah recited sawan with a ḍammah on the sīn; the rest with a kasrah. Both are dialects, like ʿidan and ʿidan, and ṭuwa and ṭuwa.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: a just place between us and you. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a clear open place. al-Kalbi said: other than this place. Abu ʿUbayd and al-Qaysi said: a middle point between the two groups. Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi said:

"Indeed our father had settled in a town
equidistant between Qays and Qays of ʿAylan, and al-Fazar."

Al-Fazar: Saʿd ibn Zayd Manat.

He (Moses) said: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: that is, the Day of ʿAshura'.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was a festival day for them every year, when they would adorn themselves and gather.

Jaʿfar related from Saʿid, who said: it was a market day for them. It was also said: it was the day of Nawruz.

Al-Hasan and Hubayrah on the authority of Hafs recited ﴿yawm al-zinah﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning "on the day"; the rest recited it with ḍammah as a subject and predicate.

﴿And that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾: at the time of mid-morning, when they gather openly in daylight, so that the proof is more conclusive and further from doubt. ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his scheme﴾, his tricks, and his sorcerers. ﴿Then he came to the appointment.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they were seventy-two sorcerers, each with a rope and a staff. It was also said they were four hundred.

Moses said to the sorcerers: ﴿Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾. The people of Kufa recited ﴿fayuḥṭikakum﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā' [[In the Isfahan copy: the tā'.]] and a kasrah on the ḥā'; the rest with a fatḥah on both. Both are dialects: saḥta and asḥta.

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿will destroy you﴾; Qatadah said: will root you out; Abu Salih said: will slaughter you. al-Farazdaq said:

"The age has bitten, O son of Marwan, and left
of wealth only what is wiped out or what is worn away."
[[Kitab al-ʿAyn: 2/224.]] [[In the Isfahan copy: "only what is a trace or swears."]]

﴿Then they disputed their affair among themselves and conferred in secret﴾: al-najwa means private conversation, and it may be a noun or a verbal noun. ﴿They said: "Indeed these two are only sorcerers."﴾ ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud) recited: "wa-asarru al-najwa, inna hadhani la-sahiran" with the alif of inna pronounced with a fatḥah and the nūn of ḥadhani... Ibn Kathir and Hafs recited ﴿inna hadhani la-sahirani﴾ with a kasrah on the alif of inna and a jazm on the nūn, with the alif in hadhani, meaning "these two are nothing but sorcerers," like the saying: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 186]. [[In the Isfahan copy an addition: meaning: we do not think you are other than among the liars.]] A poet said:

"May your mother lose you, for you have killed none but a Muslim;
the punishment of the Merciful has descended upon you."

Meaning: you have killed none but a Muslim. The validity of this reading is supported by the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "inna dhan la-sahiran" [[In the Isfahan copy: "inna dhan la-sahiran."]]. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafi and Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ [[In the Isfahan copy: Abu ʿAmr al-ʿAlaʾ.]] recited "inna hadhayni la-sahiran" with a yā', according to the original form. Abu ʿAmr said: "I am ashamed before God to recite 'inna hadhani'." The rest recited inna with tashdid and hadhani with an alif, and they differed about it.

Some people said, based on what Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbdus and ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamid told us, that they said: Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Asamm narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm al-Samari narrated to us, saying: al-Farra' narrated to us, saying: Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿAʾishah, that she was asked about God's saying in al-Nisa': ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 162], and about His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], and about His saying: ﴿Indeed these two are sorcerers﴾ [Taha: 63]. She said: "O nephew, this is an error of the scribe."

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan said: "There is a solecism in the Mushaf, and the Arabs will correct it with their tongues."

Aban said: this verse was recited in front of ʿUthman, and he said: "A solecism and an error." It was said to him: "Why did you not change it?" He said:
"Leave it, for it does not make lawful what is forbidden, nor forbid what is lawful."
